analysis|03-14|1883|Πεθαίνει ο Καρλ Μαρξ|Death of Karl Marx|Karl Marx died on 14 March 1883 in London, where he had lived in exile for decades. He had collaborated with Friedrich Engels on the Communist Manifesto, a text that became fundamental to the socialist movement. His life was bound up with the economic analysis of his age. // His funeral took place at the Highgate cemetery with a small gathering, as most of his comrades were scattered. Engels gave the funeral oration, and the scene symbolised the loneliness of the end. // His thought was deeply influential in the social sciences. His works, especially Capital, shaped political thought, labour movements and the revolutions of the twentieth century, and the discussions continue today.

analysis|03-14|1885|Πρεμιέρα του «Μικάντο»|Premiere of The Mikado|The musical The Mikado by Gilbert and Sullivan opened at the Savoy Theatre in London on 14 March 1885. The satire referred to British administration and manners, with a Japanese setting. The choice of setting was a way for the work to speak about British society. // The production was a great success and remained on continuous tour. The audiences of the time embraced the music and the humour of the work. // The collaborators created a new type of light opera that combined music and satirical speech. The work became one of the most beloved of its era and is still staged in theatres and amateur venues.

analysis|03-14|2018|Πεθαίνει ο Στίβεν Χόκινγκ|Death of Stephen Hawking|Stephen Hawking died in Cambridge on 14 March 2018, at the age of 76. Suffering from a rare motor neurone disease, he continued to work with special communication systems. The illness did not prevent him from remaining active in science. // He studied black holes and their evaporation through quantum theory, a result known as Hawking radiation. This work connected general relativity with quantum physics. // His books were addressed to a wide audience. His scientific legacy and his personal story continue to influence public debate about science and disability.

analysis|03-15|-44|Δολοφονείται ο Ιούλιος Καίσαρας|Julius Caesar Is Assassinated|On 15 March 44 BC Julius Caesar was murdered in the Senate in Rome by a group of senators who feared the concentration of power in his hands. Caesar had been declared dictator for life shortly before. That decision heightened the anxiety of his political opponents. // The conspirators stabbed him many times, and he is said to have fallen at the base of the chamber. The scene remained in memory as the most dramatic act of public life in Rome. // The day became known as the Ides of March. The murder did not save the Roman Republic, because civil wars followed and the establishment of Augustus as the first emperor.

analysis|03-15|1493|Ο Κολόμβος επιστρέφει στην Ισπανία|Columbus Returns to Spain|On 15 March 1493 Christopher Columbus reached the port of Palos in Spain, after returning from his first voyage. The return was swift, despite the storms he had faced in the Atlantic. The arrival became one of the most important naval achievements of the age. // Columbus then presented to the monarchs of Castile the discovery of islands that he had believed to be near Asia. The announcement made a great impression in Europe. // His subsequent voyages opened North and South America to European expansion, with serious and disastrous consequences for the indigenous peoples. The history of his voyages remains a subject of historical judgement.

analysis|03-15|1917|Παραιτείται ο τσάρος Νικόλαος Β΄|Tsar Nicholas II Abdicates|On 15 March 1917 Tsar Nicholas II abdicated, after the uprising in Petrograd and the defection of the troops. The abdication was made in favour of his brother, who however refused the power. The crisis had developed into political collapse. // The Romanov monarchy came to an end, and a provisional government took over the administration. The tsar and his family were placed under arrest. // The change did not bring stability, and the contradictions between the provisional government and the soviets led to the October Revolution. The period is connected with the changes that marked the twentieth century.

analysis|03-15|1922|Ο Φουάντ Α΄ γίνεται βασιλιάς της Αιγύπτου|Fuad I Becomes King of Egypt|In 1922 Egypt was recognised as an independent state by Britain, by a unilateral declaration. Sultan Fuad I was proclaimed king and the country became an independent kingdom. The change was the result of political pressure from the Egyptians. // The independence was limited, as Britain retained control of defence, the Suez Canal and foreign relations. The king had power over many matters, but parliament and the parties were strong. // The regime lasted until the revolution of 1952, and the period left a long debate about real independence. The experience influenced Egyptian politics for decades.

analysis|03-15|1939|Η Γερμανία καταλαμβάνει την Τσεχία|Germany Occupies Czechia|On 15 March 1939 Hitler occupied Czechoslovakia, breaking the Munich Agreement of 1938. German forces entered Prague, and Bohemia and Moravia were placed under German protection. The move was a clear violation of international agreements. // Britain and France reacted with protests, but the occupation took place without serious resistance. Slovakia became a dependent state, and the balance of the region changed. // The move showed that the policy of appeasement had failed, and soon Germany began the invasion of Poland, leading to the Second World War. The occupation of Prague is regarded as a milestone in the escalation towards war.

analysis|03-16|1521|Ο Μαγγελάνος φτάνει στις Φιλιππίνες|Magellan Reaches the Philippines|On 16 March 1521 Magellan arrived at the island of Samar in the Philippines, during his voyage around the world. The expedition had set out from Spain in 1519. The voyage was one of the most ambitious of the era. // Contact with the locals was initially friendly, and Magellan took part in alliances with local rulers. These alliances were connected with the political games of the region. // The religious and political influence of the Spaniards began to take root on the islands. This contact opened the way to the long Spanish presence in the Philippines. // The expedition contributed to the understanding that the Earth is round, but Magellan himself was killed in a clash shortly afterwards. His companions completed the circumnavigation, and the success remained in the memory of seafaring.

analysis|03-16|1926|Ο Ρόμπερτ Γκόνταρντ εκτοξεύει τον πρώτο πύραυλο υγρών καυσίμων|Robert Goddard Launches the First Liquid-Fuel Rocket|On 16 March 1926 Robert Goddard launched the first liquid-fuel rocket on his farm near Auburn, Massachusetts. The rocket rose a few metres and landed after a few seconds. The test was brief but historic. // Goddard had worked for years on rocket theory, and this test was the first practical demonstration of a liquid propellant. The progress was small but decisive for the future of spaceflight. // His work is regarded as the foundation of modern rocketry. Its importance became clear in that period, when the two superpowers were investing in space. // Later it influenced the space research programmes of both the United States and the Soviet Union. That small flight remains the starting point of a great technological journey.

analysis|03-16|1968|Η σφαγή του Μάι Λάι|The My Lai Massacre|In Vietnam, in the late 1960s, the American military operation in the area of the village of My Lai rested on the assumption that guerrillas were hiding there. The units operating in the area had very little information about the inhabitants. The lack of information led to mistakes with tragic consequences. // On 16 March 1968 soldiers killed hundreds of civilians, women, children and the elderly, and the victims were unarmed. The civilians were gathered and executed in groups, in an operation that lasted for hours. // The event became known in 1969 through journalistic investigations and strengthened the anti-war movement in the United States. One officer was tried, and the case remained a symbol of war crimes.

analysis|03-17|1861|Ανακηρύσσεται το Βασίλειο της Ιταλίας|The Kingdom of Italy Is Proclaimed|On 17 March 1861 parliament proclaimed the Kingdom of Italy, with Victor Emmanuel II as king. By 1861 the government of Piedmont, headed by Cavour, had united with the help of Garibaldi's volunteers a large part of Italy. Venice still belonged to Austria and Rome was under the protection of the Pope. The proclamation was the result of long negotiations. // The proclamation took place without Venice and Rome, which had not yet been incorporated. The new state began with a limited territory. // Unification was completed later, with Venice in 1866 and Rome in 1870. The new state faced great problems in integrating the different regions and in the economic inequality between North and South.

analysis|03-17|1958|Εκτοξεύεται το Vanguard 1|Vanguard 1 Is Launched|On 17 March 1958 the United States launched the satellite Vanguard 1, after earlier unsuccessful attempts. The mission was part of the programme for the International Geophysical Year. The launch had a scientific character. // The satellite was small, with solar arrays that powered its instruments, and it transmitted temperature measurements. It operated for several years and showed the potential of solar cells in space. // The satellite remains in orbit and is the oldest man-made object in space, while its technology influenced the next NASA programmes. Its presence recalls the birth of the space age.

analysis|03-17|1966|Βρίσκεται η χαμένη βόμβα υδρογόνου της Παλομάρες|The Lost Hydrogen Bomb of Palomares Is Found|On 17 March 1966 an American submarine located, in the sea off Andalusia, the nuclear bomb that had fallen after the collision of two aircraft over Palomares. The collision had taken place at the beginning of 1966, about two months earlier. The incident was of great importance for international relations. // Recovering the bomb was difficult, as it lay at great depth. The operation relied on special equipment and teams of divers, who worked under difficult conditions. // The incident highlighted the dangers of transporting nuclear weapons by air. Public opinion became anxious about the safety of nuclear weapons. // It led to stricter safety procedures and greater care in the transport of nuclear weapons. The episode remains a reminder of the dangers of the period.

analysis|03-17|1969|Η Γκόλντα Μέιρ πρωθυπουργός|Golda Meir Becomes Prime Minister|On 17 March 1969 Golda Meir took office as Prime Minister of Israel, the first woman to hold the post. The succession came after the death of Levi Eshkol. Her election was an important event for the political life of the country. // During her term the country faced the Yom Kippur War of 1973, and her leadership was criticised for its decisions. This crisis affected her position in political life. // Her term remains a point of reference for the participation of women in the politics of Israel and the Middle East. Her presence opened the way for other women in the politics of the region.

analysis|03-18|1871|Αρχίζει η Κομμούνα του Παρισιού|The Paris Commune Begins|On 18 March 1871 the government's army tried to seize the cannons of the National Guard in Paris, but the inhabitants resisted and held the city. The Paris Commune was founded as a revolutionary administration. The event was a direct consequence of the defeat by Prussia and of the political crisis that followed. // The Commune introduced measures of social reform and the election of officials. Its operation was based on local assemblies and the participation of citizens. // Its power lasted two months, and the government army overthrew it by force. The repression was harsh, with thousands dead and arrested. // The Commune acquired great symbolic significance for the labour movement, and the experience remained in the memory of the revolutionaries as the first example of workers' power.

analysis|03-18|1921|Η συνθήκη της Ρίγας|The Treaty of Riga|On 18 March 1921 Poland and Soviet Russia signed the Treaty of Riga, after military clashes. The agreement set the eastern borders of Poland. The treaty was the result of the Polish-Soviet War of the period. // The treaty included arrangements for prisoners and mutual recognition. The arrangement gave a form of peace to the troubled region. // Poland kept territories with a large population of Belarusian and Ukrainian origin. The decision left long-lasting tensions with its neighbours. // These borders remained essentially as they were until the Second World War and affected the geopolitics of the region for decades.

analysis|03-18|1922|Καταδικάζεται ο Γκάντι|Gandhi Is Sentenced|On 18 March 1922 Gandhi was tried in India for civil disobedience and sentenced to six years in prison. He stated in court that he could not deny that he was consciously breaking the law. His attitude became a point of reference for the movement. // He was released early after a surgical operation, having served only part of the sentence. The trial strengthened his image as a leader of the resistance. // The case became a symbol of colonial oppression, and it was linked with later protests and the negotiations for independence. Gandhi's figure remained central throughout the path to Indian independence.

analysis|03-18|1962|Οι Συμφωνίες του Εβιάν|The Évian Accords|On 18 March 1962 the agreements that ended the war in Algeria were signed at Évian in France. France recognised the independence of the country after seven years of conflict. The agreement was the result of long negotiations. // The agreements provided for a ceasefire, the protection of French citizens and a procedure for a referendum. The reaction of the French military circles was strong. // Independence opened a new period for Algeria, while migration between the two countries remained a permanent feature of their relations. The agreement remains in history as a milestone of decolonisation.

analysis|03-18|1965|Ο Αλεξέι Λεόνοφ κάνει τον πρώτο διαστημικό περίπατο|Alexei Leonov Makes the First Spacewalk|On 18 March 1965 Alexei Leonov left the spacecraft Voskhod 2 and carried out the first spacewalk. The exit lasted a few minutes, and the cosmonaut was tethered to the craft. The act opened a new path for space missions. // The mission was dangerous, because the suit had inflated and returning to the craft became very difficult. Leonov managed to return, with determination and composure. // The success strengthened the Soviet space programme, and the spacewalk became a milestone for later missions. The experience was decisive for the design of later space exits.

analysis|03-18|2014|Η Ρωσία προσαρτά την Κριμαία|Russia Annexes Crimea|On 18 March 2014 Russia signed the treaty for the annexation of Crimea, a few days after the referendum in the region. Ukraine and most countries did not recognise the outcome. The international reaction was immediate and strong. // The referendum was held under military presence, something that was questioned internationally. Russia invoked the protection of Russian-speaking citizens, an argument that many countries did not accept. // The annexation led to sanctions and to long-lasting tension between Russia and the West, and Crimea remains a central issue in their relations. This affair changed European security.

analysis|03-19|1812|Το Σύνταγμα του Κάδιθ|The Constitution of Cádiz|On 19 March 1812 Spain was under French occupation, while the government in Cádiz, one of the few cities still resisting, operated as a centre of the liberals. The deputies wanted to limit royal power and establish national sovereignty. The situation of the country favoured liberal ideas. // The General Cortes voted the Constitution of Cádiz, which set out a constitutional monarchy, national sovereignty and universal male suffrage for the indirect electors. The text was among the most progressive of its time. // The Constitution was in force for a limited period, because Ferdinand VII abolished it in 1814. Nevertheless, it became a model for liberal movements in Spain, Italy and Greece. Its influence was greater than its duration.

analysis|03-19|1931|Η Νεβάδα νομιμοποιεί τον τζόγο|Nevada Legalises Gambling|On 19 March 1931 the state of Nevada, which faced economic difficulties, was seeking sources of revenue. Gambling was illegal in almost all US states at the time. The legislative change was a bold step for the period. // Nevada's legislation legalised casinos and gambling, and so the state became for several years the only one with legal gambling on a large scale. The decision gave the state a unique feature. // That legislation provided the basis for the development of Las Vegas, which became one of the best-known entertainment cities in the world. The related debates about the economy and the social impact of gambling continue.

analysis|03-19|1944|Οι Ναζί καταλαμβάνουν την Ουγγαρία|The Nazis Occupy Hungary|In March 1944 German forces occupied Hungary, which until then had been an ally of the Axis, because the country's leadership was negotiating an exit from the war. Hitler wanted to secure control of the country. The occupation radically changed the political situation. // The occupation brought Adolf Eichmann and the deportation records, and within the following months almost four hundred thousand Jews were deported, mainly to Auschwitz. The massacre in the Hungarian countryside was among the largest of the Holocaust. // After the war Hungary found itself in the Soviet sphere of influence, and responsibility for the deportations was analysed by courts and historians for decades. This history remains heavy in the memory of the country.

analysis|03-19|1962|Το πρώτο άλμπουμ του Μπομπ Ντύλαν|Bob Dylan's First Album|On 19 March 1962 Bob Dylan's first record, titled Bob Dylan, was released in the United States. The young singer had moved to New York and was performing in small cafés of Greenwich Village. The beginning of his career was relatively modest. // The album contained mainly covers of traditional songs and very few original ones, and its production was limited. Its commercial success was modest. // The record was the start of a career that changed folk music and pop, and Dylan later became a Nobel laureate in Literature. That first release remains a starting point.

analysis|03-19|1982|Οι Αργεντινοί αποβιβάζονται στη Νότια Γεωργία|Argentines Land on South Georgia|On 19 March 1982 Argentine workers landed on South Georgia in the South Atlantic, with permission from the government, to dismantle an old whaling station. The British and Argentine administrations had disagreed over the islands since the nineteenth century. That disagreement had deep roots. // This action, without clear permission from the British authorities, provoked reactions and tension. Britain demanded the withdrawal of those who had landed. // The crisis preceded the invasion of the Falkland Islands shortly afterwards and the war that followed in 1982. The episode is regarded as the start of the escalation.

analysis|03-20|1815|Ο Ναπολέων επιστρέφει στο Παρίσι|Napoleon Returns to Paris|On 20 March 1815 Napoleon returned to Paris after Louis XVIII had fled, and the Hundred Days began. The army welcomed him and the king fled to Ghent. The return took place without serious resistance. // The allies of Europe declared Napoleon an enemy, and armies gathered in Belgium. That decision showed the determination of the powers of the Congress of Vienna. // Napoleon moved against them, and the clash took place in early June. That move was his last great operation. // The defeat at Waterloo in June 1815 ended the period of the Hundred Days and led to Napoleon's exile on Saint Helena. The period remains in history as a brief but dramatic episode.

analysis|03-20|1852|Εκδίδεται η «Καλύβα του Μπάρμπα-Θωμά»|Uncle Tom's Cabin Is Published|On 20 March 1852 Harriet Beecher Stowe's novel Uncle Tom's Cabin was published, describing the life of enslaved people in the South. The book was written as a reaction to slavery and to the Fugitive Slave Act. The work was a political act as literature. // Its success was enormous, and millions of copies were sold in the United States and Europe. Its readership went beyond the country's borders. // The work became the subject of intense debate, since its narratives also contained stereotypical images. This criticism was linked with the wider confrontation over slavery. // The cabin gave new impetus to the anti-slavery movement, and its influence on public opinion was significant before the Civil War.

analysis|03-20|1916|Ο Αϊνστάιν δημοσιεύει τη Γενική Θεωρία της Σχετικότητας|Einstein Publishes the General Theory of Relativity|On 20 March 1916 Albert Einstein published in the journal Annalen der Physik the general theory of relativity, which described gravity as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass. The theory was an extension of the special theory of 1905. The publication took place in the midst of the war. // The theory predicted phenomena that could be tested, such as the deflection of light by the Sun. In 1919 observations during a solar eclipse confirmed the prediction. // The theory changed physics and cosmology, and led to the study of black holes and gravitational waves. The confirmation of 1919 became one of the best-known scientific events of the century.

analysis|03-20|1956|Η Τυνησία γίνεται ανεξάρτητη|Tunisia Becomes Independent|On 20 March 1956 Tunisia proclaimed its independence from France, after negotiations with the French government. Habib Bourguiba, the leader of the movement, became the first president of the country. The independence was the result of long national pressure. // The independence came from long political pressure and from the agreements of 1955 with France. The negotiations lasted years and included reforms in education and administration. // The country followed a policy with an emphasis on modernising education, and it remains one of the states that maintained relative stability in North Africa. The history of its independence is linked with the modern course of the country.

analysis|03-20|1995|Η επίθεση με αέριο σαρίν στο μετρό του Τόκιο|The Sarin Gas Attack on the Tokyo Subway|On 20 March 1995 members of the Aum Shinrikyo sect released the nerve agent sarin in subway trains in Tokyo during the morning rush hour. The attack killed thirteen people and injured thousands. The scale of the attack was unprecedented. // The perpetrators used bags of the gas, which they pierced with umbrellas, in several trains at the same time. The police and rescue workers faced a lack of information about the nature of the substance. // The attack led to the arrest and trial of the sect's leaders, and to changes in anti-terrorism measures and in the handling of chemical threats. The event remains a lesson for cities.

analysis|03-20|2003|Αρχίζει η εισβολή στο Ιράκ|The Invasion of Iraq Begins|On 20 March 2003 the United States and its allies began an operation in Iraq, aiming to overthrow Saddam Hussein. The intervention was based on the claim that weapons of mass destruction existed, a claim that was not confirmed later. The international community had been divided over its legitimacy. // The forces entered the country quickly and took Baghdad within a few weeks. The regime collapsed, and Hussein was overthrown. // The intervention led to long-term instability, to civil conflicts and to the rise of Islamist organisations. Criticism of the legitimacy and preparation of the invasion remains intense.

analysis|03-21|1685|Γεννιέται ο Γιόχαν Σεμπάστιαν Μπαχ|Johann Sebastian Bach Is Born|On 21 March 1685 Johann Sebastian Bach was born in Eisenach in Thuringia, a member of a family of musicians with a long tradition. His father was a musician at the local court. The family environment shaped his musical path. // Bach worked as an organist and composer in churches and courts in Germany, and in Leipzig he was cantor of the Thomasschule. He wrote works for orchestra, organ and voice, such as the Brandenburg Concertos and the Passions. // His work is regarded as the summit of the Baroque, and his influence on Western music continues to this day, with constant performances and studies. His music remains a central part of the repertoire.

analysis|03-21|1960|Η σφαγή στο Σάρπβιλ|The Sharpeville Massacre|In South Africa the apartheid regime imposed laws that restricted black citizens in movement, work and voting, through the so-called passes. The residents of Sharpeville had organised a peaceful protest against the laws. That protest was one of the best-known acts of resistance of the period. // On 21 March 1960 the police opened fire on demonstrators outside the Sharpeville police station, and sixty-nine people were killed. The number of wounded was also large. // The event caused international outrage and led to the banning of the African National Congress and the suspension of many anti-apartheid organisations. 21 March became a day of remembrance of human rights in South Africa.

analysis|03-21|1963|Κλείνει η φυλακή του Αλκατράζ|Alcatraz Prison Closes|Alcatraz was a prison on an island in San Francisco Bay, known for the severity of its regime and for its famous inmates. Its operation was costly, and the building had deteriorated from the marine environment. The prison had become a symbol of harshness. // The prison closed in March 1963 and the inmates were moved to other institutions. That situation ended an era. // The buildings stood empty for years. In 1972 the island was incorporated into the Golden Gate National Recreation Area, and today it is a popular tourist destination and a symbol of the city's history.

analysis|03-21|1965|Η πορεία από τη Σέλμα στο Μοντγκόμερι|The Selma to Montgomery March|On 21 March 1965 Martin Luther King led the third march from Selma to Montgomery, Alabama, for voting rights. The march was protected by federal troops and the National Guard. That march was a turning point for the movement. // The demonstrators set out with a few hundred and reached Montgomery with thousands of participants, in a march that lasted five days. The escort of military units ensured their safety. // The march led to the passage of the Voting Rights Act in August 1965, which removed many obstacles to the registration of black voters. The march remains in history as a symbol of non-violent struggle.

analysis|03-21|1999|Περιήγηση της Γης με αερόστατο|Balloon Circumnavigation of the Earth|On 21 March 1999 Bertrand Piccard and Brian Jones completed the first non-stop balloon circumnavigation of the Earth, with the Breitling Orbiter 3. The flight began in the Alps of Switzerland and lasted almost twenty days. That success was a great achievement of aeronautics. // The balloon flew over the Pacific and the Indian Ocean, and landed in the Egyptian desert or near it, relative to the original forecasts. The technique of the flight relied on air currents at different altitudes. // The success of the mission showed the possibility of long-duration human flights by balloon, and inspired new efforts in aeronautics. The flight remains a landmark of the era.

analysis|03-22|1895|Οι αδελφοί Λυμιέρ προβάλλουν την πρώτη ταινία|The Lumière Brothers Screen the First Film|On 22 March 1895 the Lumière brothers gave a private screening of a cinematographic film in Paris, titled Workers Leaving the Factory. The screening took place at the Société d'encouragement pour l'industrie nationale. That screening was one of the first public presentations of cinema. // The spectators saw short frames of workers leaving a factory, and the image moved before them for a few minutes. The event was considered innovative for the time. // The invention of cinema opened the way to the entertainment industry, and the Lumière brothers are regarded as pioneers of the form. The history of cinema begins with that screening.

analysis|03-22|1933|Ανοίγει το στρατόπεδο του Νταχάου|Dachau Concentration Camp Opens|On 22 March 1933 the Dachau concentration camp, near Munich, was opened, the first that the Nazi regime operated. Initially it housed political opponents, communists and social democrats. Its operation was the first form of the systematic repression that would follow. // Prisoners were subjected to hard labour, violence and humiliation by the guards. Over the years the camp became a centre for training the guards of the other camps. // Dachau became the model for the regime's later camps, and more than one hundred thousand people passed through it. Its operation showed how quickly violence could be institutionalised. // Today it operates as a memorial, and visitors learn there about the victims and about the mechanisms that enabled the crimes. The site is one of the most important places of memory in Europe.

analysis|03-22|1945|Ιδρύεται ο Αραβικός Σύνδεσμος|The Arab League Is Founded|On 22 March 1945 seven Arab states, among them Egypt, Syria and Iraq, signed in Cairo the charter of the Arab League. The founding was the result of a common need for coordination in the region, at a time when the war was ending. The initiative showed a desire for cooperation. // The League aimed at cooperation among states on political, economic and cultural matters, while preserving the national sovereignty of its members. That principle set the limits of cooperation. // The Arab League operates to this day, based in Cairo, and its influence on the diplomacy of the region remains significant. Its decisions often reflect the internal balances of its members.

analysis|03-22|1963|Το πρώτο άλμπουμ των Beatles|The Beatles' First Album|On 22 March 1963 the first album of the Beatles, titled Please Please Me, was released in Britain, recorded in a few hours. The group already had hits as singles and often performed in Britain. That recording moment was decisive for their path. // The album mainly contained original songs by Lennon and McCartney and quickly became a great success. Production took place at an intense pace, and success came quickly. // It was one of the first examples of British beat music. The release was the start of the British Invasion in the United States, and the group deeply influenced modern pop music.

analysis|03-23|1839|Πρώτη γραπτή χρήση του «ΟΚ»|First Recorded Use of OK|On 23 March 1839 the Boston Morning Post newspaper published "OK" as an abbreviation of "all correct", in an article about the linguistic fashion of the time. The phrase was already in use in informal speech. The publication gave the abbreviation public visibility. // The abbreviation spread in newspapers and then in speech, with various explanations for its origin. The fashion for abbreviations was intense in that period. // The exact origin remains a subject of debate. Today "OK" is one of the most widespread words in the world and is used in many languages.

analysis|03-23|1857|Το πρώτο ασανσέρ της Otis|Otis's First Passenger Elevator|On 23 March 1857 Elisha Otis installed in a New York building the first passenger elevator with a safety mechanism, which stopped automatically if the cable broke. The mechanism changed the design of tall buildings. The need for safe lifts was pressing. // The installation took place at the Haughwout store, and Otis demonstrated the safety of the system to the public. That demonstration gave people confidence in the technology. // The invention reduced people's fear of lifts and made the construction of skyscrapers possible. The Otis company became one of the largest in the sector.

analysis|03-23|1919|Ο Μουσολίνι ιδρύει το φασιστικό κίνημα|Mussolini Founds the Fascist Movement|On 23 March 1919 Benito Mussolini founded in Milan the Fasci di Combattimento, an organisation of former soldiers and nationalists with a rhetoric opposed to socialism. The group was founded in a period of great social unrest. That organisation was the first step of the fascist movement. // The group appeared in political life after the First World War, with violent actions against labour organisations. That violence became a characteristic of its activity. // The fascist Fasci formed the core of the fascist movement, which seized power in Italy in 1922. That original group became the basis for the rise of the regime.

analysis|03-23|1933|Ο Νόμος περί Εξουσιοδότησης|The Enabling Act|On 23 March 1933 the Reichstag passed the Enabling Act, which allowed Hitler and his government to legislate without the participation of parliament for four years. The vote took place under pressure, with the Communist deputies unable to take part. That situation showed the erosion of democratic institutions. // The Centre supported the law after assurances, and that decision remained controversial. That support in practice legitimised the shift of power. // The law handed the Nazi government dictatorial powers and effectively ended the Weimar Republic. That vote is among the most critical moments in German history.

analysis|03-23|1965|Η πτήση του Gemini 3|The Gemini 3 Flight|On 23 March 1965 Gemini 3 was launched with astronauts Gus Grissom and John Young, as the first American mission with two astronauts. The mission lasted three orbits around the Earth. The mission opened a new chapter in American spaceflight. // Young presented a small sandwich to the crew, an event that Congress later discussed. The incident became more widely known and recalls the human side of the missions. // The spacecraft was successfully tested.
